patches.old: Higher post-evolution scores raise an identification question: what improvement is carried by the persistent skill, and what remains useful after the task changes? We examine this question through a diagnosis of SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills, connecting their construction procedures, completed artifacts, and downstream behavior. Repeated paired evaluations establish source-task utility, controlled variations probe its scope, and skill contents and execution traces explain contrasting reuse outcomes. The evidence separates recurring benchmark gains from reusable decision guidance: positive source-task benefits coexist with sharply different responses to changed instances and requirements. Successful cases preserve criteria for selecting valid results and maintaining task constraints. This analysis connects observed gains to what the skill helps an executor decide, making behavioral persistence and attribution central to evaluating skill learning.
patches.new: Self-evolving agents store experience in persistent skills, but a higher task score leaves open what the skill has learned. We study whether the resulting benefit persists beyond the source task and which decisions in the skill explain its success or failure. Our diagnosis follows SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills from skill construction to frozen deployment, combining repeated paired evaluations, controlled task variations, and inspection of skill contents and execution traces. Source-task gains recur across all three methods, while changed tasks expose different scopes of useful reuse. Contrasting cases locate this difference in how skills distinguish valid answers from plausible candidates and preserve the constraints that define a correct solution. The findings connect benchmark gains to persistent decision guidance and distinguish producing a useful skill, applying its guidance, and sustaining its benefit under task change.

patches.old:
Agent skills externalize behavior into persistent instructions, scripts, and references that can be inspected and reused without changing model parameters. SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills construct these artifacts from execution experience through deployment-grounded revision, verified-trajectory distillation, and co-evolutionary verification~\cite{zhang2026skillevolver,zhou2026spark,zhang2026coevoskills}. A higher score after this process raises the question in our title: what has the system learned as a skill?

The final score is produced through several steps. Construction determines which guidance enters the artifact; the executor decides how to use that guidance; and a verifier assesses the resulting output. A skill can preserve a useful decision rule, an instance-specific choice, or instructions that a later executor applies incompletely. These possibilities can yield similar source-task scores while producing different behavior when the input or requirement changes. Locating the improvement therefore requires examining the persistent artifact together with its deployment.

We pursue two connected research objectives. First, we examine whether completed skills provide recurring utility and how far that utility extends under controlled task variation. Second, we investigate which decisions preserved in the skills help explain successful and failed reuse, and how those decisions relate to the feedback used during construction. This keeps the existence and scope of a benefit separate from the explanation of how it arises.

Our empirical diagnosis begins with two standard-task runs per method, pairing each skill condition with a no-skill execution of the same task. We then apply frozen skills to changes in input representation, task instances, and coupled requirements. Finally, contrasting signal-detection and scheduling cases connect the observed outcomes to the guidance used by the executor. The sequence links the score, the conditions under which it persists, and the decisions carried by the artifact.

The central finding is a separation between recurring source-task benefit and reusable behavior. All three methods have positive paired mean gains in both standard-task runs, but this agreement breaks under task variation. SkillEvolver remains positive across all three change types; SPARK and CoEvoSkills lose utility on replacement instances. The cases reveal a corresponding distinction in skill content: finding a plausible signal differs from identifying the required signal, and constructing a feasible schedule differs from preserving the rules of an acceptable repair. Successful reuse accompanies guidance that retains these distinctions.

We contribute an empirical diagnosis of the persistence of completed-skill utility and an analysis of the decision guidance preserved in successful reuse. The repeated outcomes establish utility at deployment; controlled variations reveal its behavioral scope; and artifact and trace evidence connect that scope to reusable decision criteria. Together, these observations address what benchmark gains say about skill learning.

Persistent agent skills offer a route to improvement without updating model parameters. Instructions, scripts, and supporting references make execution experience available to later runs. SkillEvolver, SPARK, and CoEvoSkills construct these artifacts through deployment-grounded revision, verified-trajectory distillation, and co-evolutionary verification~\cite{zhang2026skillevolver,zhou2026spark,zhang2026coevoskills}. Their outputs motivate the question in our title: when a system produces a higher-scoring skill, what useful behavior has become persistent?

The location of that improvement matters. A skill can preserve a decision rule that remains useful on new inputs, a choice tailored to the original instance, or a check that a later executor fails to apply. These artifacts may all help on the source task, yet lead to different outcomes when the task changes. The final score also combines artifact construction, execution, and verification. Understanding skill learning therefore requires following the stored guidance into the behavior it supports.

We ask two connected questions. \textbf{Does the benefit persist, and under which task changes?} Repeated source-task evaluations test whether paired utility recurs, while frozen-skill variants expose the demands that the same guidance can accommodate. \textbf{What in the skill and its use explains the observed outcomes?} Contrasting executions reveal whether decisive correctness criteria are available in the skill and applied to the new task. These questions connect the existence and scope of useful behavior with an account of how it is produced.

We examine three construction mechanisms through two standard-task runs per method and controlled changes to input representation, task instances, and coupled requirements. Each skill condition is paired with a no-skill execution of the same task. Signal-detection and scheduling cases then connect the aggregate patterns to decisions visible in the skills and execution traces. The completed artifact is the common object of diagnosis: its construction provides context, and its later use supplies the behavioral evidence.

All three methods yield positive mean source-task gains in both runs, but this agreement does not persist under task variation. SkillEvolver remains positive across all three change types. SPARK's benefit depends on the change type, and CoEvoSkills has negative mean gains in all three. The clearest separation occurs when the instance is replaced. The cases explain why executing a procedure is only part of the problem: the executor must also distinguish the required signal from misleading candidates and a valid schedule repair from an otherwise feasible schedule.

Our contribution is a diagnosis of what observed skill gains represent. Repeated paired evaluations establish recurring utility, controlled variants locate its scope, and artifact-level cases identify decisions associated with successful and failed reuse. Together, these results show how a score advantage can be interpreted through the guidance that survives construction and is actually used during execution.

The score $V(x,A(x,s,z))$ depends jointly on the skill, its execution, and the verifier. A skill-versus-no-skill comparison measures the utility of a completed artifact at deployment. A parent-to-final comparison instead measures the change associated with revising an existing artifact. Keeping these contrasts distinct specifies which part of the learning question an evaluation answers.

Our empirical contrast is completed-skill utility. We first examine whether its paired mean is positive in each of two runs on the same task set. We then freeze the source-task skill $s_x$ and apply it to a variant $T_k(x)$, pairing its outcome with a no-skill execution on that variant. The executor can reinterpret inputs and adapt its actions; the skill itself is not revised. Persistence of utility under these changes locates the observed scope of reuse.

Attribution concerns the decisions connecting the artifact to the result. We inspect what the skill tells the executor to retain, recompute, or check, and how that guidance appears in successful and failed executions. Published construction procedures supply an explanation for how such guidance may arise. This separates observed behavior and artifact content from interpretation of the evolution pathway.

The score $V(x,A(x,s,z))$ records the outcome of a skill used by an executor and assessed by a verifier. Comparing a completed skill with no skill measures its utility at deployment. Comparing the adopted final skill with its actual parent addresses the improvement associated with revision. The experiments here follow the first contrast across repeated runs and changed tasks.

For each source task $x$, we freeze its completed skill $s_x$ and evaluate it on a variant $T_k(x)$ alongside a no-skill execution. The skill remains unchanged, while the executor can reinterpret the input, recompute a solution, and adapt its actions. A positive paired difference on the variant indicates that the stored guidance remains useful under that change. The variation types distinguish the decisions that can be reused from those that the executor must reconsider.

The attribution question follows the same artifact into execution. We examine which candidates its rules distinguish, which constraints its checks preserve, and where the observed behavior departs from that guidance. The construction procedures describe the feedback from which the guidance is produced. Reading these stages together connects a score change to a specific decision, rather than treating the presence of a skill file as evidence that its instructions were used effectively.

\subsection{Utility, Scope, and Attribution Answer Different Questions}

Positive paired gains in both runs establish recurring source-task utility of the completed skills. Task variation asks a different question: which parts of that usefulness survive when the original input or solution no longer suffices? The three methods agree on the first observation and diverge on the second. This is the diagnostic result behind the performance differences. A source-task average describes a benefit in one setting; the variation profile reveals what demands the same artifact can accommodate.

Average gain and improvement frequency also reveal different behavior. SPARK's slightly positive variant mean combines more regressions than improvements, so near-zero utility masks opposing changes. SkillEvolver combines a positive mean with more improvements, whereas CoEvoSkills combines a negative mean with more regressions. Pairing these summaries with the cases makes the interpretation concrete: utility depends on whether the guidance helps the executor make the changed task's decisive choices.

\subsection{What the Persistent Artifact Must Preserve}

The cases suggest that reusable skill learning preserves the relationship between a procedure and the conditions that make its result valid. In signal detection, this relationship distinguishes a target from misleading candidates. In scheduling, it connects repair actions to baseline-relative constraints. A procedure can remain executable while this relationship is lost. Conversely, a skill can guide a new solution by preserving the checks and adaptation rules that still apply.

This connects the diagnosis back to the evolution lifecycle. Feedback supplies evidence about failures; the skill expresses a rule extracted from that evidence; the executor must use it in the new setting; and the verifier records the outcome. The observed cases expose whether the guidance survives this handoff. Construction, adoption, and useful deployment are separate events, even when they contribute to the same reported score.

Evaluation should therefore follow the artifact from its source-task contribution to its changed-task behavior. Repeated paired outcomes show whether utility recurs, frozen variants test which decisions remain applicable, and skill/trace inspection explains where reuse succeeds or breaks. When the claim concerns the improvement produced by revision itself, the corresponding contrast is the actual parent and adopted final artifact. The research target is a persistent change in useful behavior, with the score serving as one observation of that change.

\subsection{A Useful Source Skill Can Have a Narrow Behavioral Scope}

The standard-task and variant results identify two properties of the completed artifacts. Source-task utility recurs for all three methods, but its scope differs under controlled changes. SkillEvolver's positive gains across P1--P3 support useful reuse under each tested change type. SPARK's positive P1 and P3 means alongside a negative P2 mean locate a more specific difficulty: adapting the representation or requirements can preserve its benefit, while replacing the underlying instance can remove it. CoEvoSkills' negative means show that guidance useful on the source task can interfere with a changed task.

Aggregate scope also contains local boundaries. SkillEvolver has the strongest P2 mean yet fails the replacement-instance signal-detection case. SPARK is nearly neutral across variants but succeeds on all three scheduling changes. These observations locate success and failure at the interaction between a skill and a task demand. The aggregate comparison reveals where to investigate; the case explains which decision remains useful or breaks.

\subsection{Correctness Criteria Must Survive Construction and Use}

The two cases expose distinct points where reuse can break. In signal detection, a procedure produces plausible candidates, but success depends on identifying which candidate satisfies the task. In scheduling, an output can satisfy structural feasibility while violating the rule that defines an acceptable repair. Reusable guidance must preserve this relationship between the procedure and its correctness criteria. The procedure's availability alone does not ensure that a later executor makes the required distinction.

This explains why inspecting the artifact and its execution together matters. CoEvoSkills contains validation checks, yet the observed executions miss decisive conditions. SkillEvolver's successful cases combine explicit decision criteria with their application to changed inputs. The contrast is between guidance as written and guidance as used: retained checks contribute only when they cover the relevant condition and are enforced during execution.

The lifecycle perspective also makes feedback informative. Deployment failures can reveal where instructions are ambiguous, verified trajectories can supply evidence for a successful procedure, and surrogate feedback can identify conditions to check. Each construction mechanism must convert that evidence into guidance that a later executor can apply. Our results locate the empirical question at this conversion and subsequent use: which decisions are preserved, when do they remain appropriate, and what happens when the executor follows them? This links the reported score back to the behavior that a persistent skill is intended to improve.

patches.old: A higher score becomes informative about skill learning when it is connected to what the persistent artifact helps an executor do. Our repeated evaluations show positive source-task utility for all three methods, while frozen task variations separate the conditions under which that utility persists. SkillEvolver retains positive gains across the three change types; SPARK and CoEvoSkills expose narrower or adverse reuse patterns. The contrasting cases connect successful reuse to criteria for identifying valid answers and preserving repair constraints. These findings distinguish useful completed artifacts, their behavioral scope, and explanations grounded in skill content. They return the learning question to persistent decision guidance: what is retained from experience, when does it remain useful, and how does it shape the next execution?
patches.new: Our diagnosis connects score gains from self-evolving skills to the behavior carried by their persistent artifacts. All three methods provide recurring source-task utility, while controlled task changes reveal sharply different scopes of reuse. SkillEvolver sustains positive average gains across representation, instance, and requirement changes; the other methods show more selective or adverse reuse. Contrasting cases locate the difference in decisions that distinguish valid answers and preserve repair constraints, including whether the executor applies the checks present in a skill. These results make the learning question concrete: experience must become useful guidance, and that guidance must continue to support correct decisions when the task changes. Evaluating skill learning therefore requires connecting construction, stored content, and observed use, with the benchmark score recording the outcome of that process.

patches.old: \section{What in the Skill Explains Its Behavior?}

The second research objective is to connect the observed outcome to the persistent guidance used during execution. Signal detection and scheduling expose two distinct decisions: selecting the valid candidate and preserving the conditions of a correct repair. We inspect both the rules written into the skills and the behavior observed when they are reused.

Signal detection tests how a skill distinguishes the required signal from plausible candidates. Scheduling tests whether a skill preserves the conditions that define an acceptable repair. In each case, we relate the rules in the artifact to their observed use.
